topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Basic geometrical ideas
topic.scope: point, line, line segment, ray, curves, polygons, angles, triangles, circles

misconceptions.statement: A line is a physical object with a specific thickness.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the mathematical concept of a line with drawn lines in notebooks.
misconceptions.fix: A mathematical line has length but no width or thickness; it is an abstract concept.

probe.question: If you zoom in on a line drawn with a pencil, does it get thicker?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is made of graphite.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

misconceptions.statement: A ray can be drawn in any direction, but it must start from the left.
misconceptions.why: Students often see rays depicted starting from the left in textbooks.
misconceptions.fix: A ray starts at a fixed point and extends infinitely in any direction.

probe.question: Is this a ray: an arrow pointing left starting from a dot?
probe.wrong_answer: No, rays must point to the right.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: The size of an angle depends on the length of the rays.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the length of the lines with the amount of rotation (opening).
misconceptions.fix: An angle is the measure of rotation between two rays; length of rays does not change the angle.

probe.question: Which angle is larger: one with 2cm rays or one with 5cm rays, both open the same amount?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: The radius is the same as the diameter.
misconceptions.why: Students often confuse the two terms because both relate to the circle's size.
misconceptions.fix: The diameter is twice the length of the radius; the radius is the distance from the center to the edge.

probe.question: If the radius is 3cm, what is the diameter?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: A line segment and a line are the same thing, so a line has two endpoints.
misconceptions.why: Students draw lines on paper with two ends and treat the drawn picture as the whole line.
misconceptions.fix: A line extends endlessly in both directions and has no endpoints. A line segment is a part of a line with two fixed endpoints.

probe.question: How many endpoints does a line passing through points A and B have?

misconceptions.root_belief: A drawn picture shows the whole object
misconceptions.source_hint: mathematics education research on geometric prototypes

misconceptions.statement: Only one line can pass through two given points, but many lines can pass through one point.
misconceptions.why: The statement is half right, and students carry the true half too far by reading 'many' as 'some' or 'none' for a single point.
misconceptions.fix: Infinitely many lines pass through one point. Exactly one line passes through two distinct points.

probe.question: How many lines can be drawn through a single point P?

misconceptions.root_belief: One point fixes exactly one line

misconceptions.statement: A line segment AB is different from a segment BA.
misconceptions.why: Students link order of letters with direction, as they do with reading and writing.
misconceptions.fix: Segment AB and segment BA are the same segment with the same endpoints and the same length. Only rays depend on which point is the starting point.

probe.question: Are segment PQ and segment QP the same? Say yes or no.
probe.wrong_answer: No, they start from different points.

misconceptions.statement: Any closed figure with straight sides is a polygon only if it looks like a regular shape, such as a regular pentagon or a regular hexagon.
misconceptions.why: Students see only regular, symmetric shapes in textbooks and posters, so they reject irregular ones.
misconceptions.fix: A polygon is any closed figure made only of line segments. Its sides can have different lengths and its angles can differ.

probe.question: A closed figure has 5 straight sides of different lengths. Is it a polygon?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because its sides are not equal.

misconceptions.root_belief: Only regular, standard-looking shapes count as examples
misconceptions.source_hint: van Hiele-based research on shape prototypes

misconceptions.statement: A triangle must have its base at the bottom and its apex pointing up.
misconceptions.why: Triangles in books are nearly always shown upright in one orientation.
misconceptions.fix: A triangle is any closed figure with three sides and three angles, in any orientation.

probe.question: A triangle is turned upside down with its point facing down. Is it still a triangle?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is not a triangle now.

misconceptions.root_belief: Shapes must appear in the standard orientation
misconceptions.source_hint: research on prototype orientation in geometry

misconceptions.statement: A closed curve must be a circle or an oval, so a figure with sharp corners cannot be a closed curve.
misconceptions.why: The word 'curve' suggests a smooth, bent line, so students think straight parts rule a figure out.
misconceptions.fix: A curve can have straight parts and corners. If it begins and ends at the same point without a gap, it is a closed curve, and a triangle or a square is one.

probe.question: Is a square a closed curve?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is not round or curved.

misconceptions.root_belief: The word curve means smooth and bending

misconceptions.statement: A curve that crosses itself is not a curve, and a curve that is not closed has to be an open curve.
misconceptions.why: Students split curves into 'neat' simple ones and 'tangled' ones, and they equate any curve not closed with a simple open one.
misconceptions.fix: A curve may cross itself. It is open if its ends do not meet, and closed if it starts and ends at the same point, whether or not it crosses itself.

probe.question: A figure-8 curve starts and ends at the same point. Is it open or closed?
probe.wrong_answer: It is not a curve, because it crosses itself.

misconceptions.root_belief: Proper curves must be simple and tidy

misconceptions.statement: The diameter of a circle can be drawn from any point on the circle to any other point on it, so it need not pass through the centre.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up chords with diameters because both join two points on the circle.
misconceptions.fix: A diameter is a line segment through the centre with both endpoints on the circle. A segment joining two points that misses the centre is not a diameter and is shorter than the diameter.

probe.question: A segment joins two points on a circle but does not pass through the centre. Is it a diameter?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both its ends are on the circle.

misconceptions.root_belief: Any segment joining two circle points is the diameter
